docs.title: Philter
docs.text:
This documentation applies to Philter 4.0.0. If you are upgrading to this version see Upgrading.

Philter is an API-based application that finds and redacts sensitive information, such as protected health information (PHI) and personally identifiable information (PII), and user-defined sensitive information from natural language text. Philter is ideal for usage in text processing pipelines where sensitive information needs removed, encrypted, or redacted from the text.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
To get going fast, jump to one of the Quick Starts:

  • Philter Quick Start on AWS
  • Philter Quick Start on Google Cloud
  • Philter Quick Start on Microsoft Azure

docs.title: Open Source
docs.text: Philter is open source software.

docs.title: Auditing
docs.text:
Philter records security-relevant actions to an audit log so you can review who did what, and when. The audit log is written to Philter's database and is intended to support security review, compliance, and incident investigation.

Audit events are either security events or redaction-activity events. Security events are always recorded: there is no setting to disable them or the audit log. The redaction-activity events (document_redaction_initiated and document_redaction_completed) can be switched off with AUDIT_REDACTION_EVENTS_ENABLED=false; see Settings.

docs.title: Where audit events are stored
docs.text:
Audit events are written to audit_events in Philter's database: a collection with MongoDB storage, a table with SQLite (see Database). Each event has the following fields:

Field Description event The type of action (one of the event names listed below). request_id A correlation id for the request or operation that produced the event. For an API request, it is the id returned in the response's X-Request-Id header, and every event the request causes shares it, except the two redaction events, which use the document id so a queued redaction's start and completion share one id. api_key_id The principal the event is recorded under, when known. Usually the calling user's id; administrative changes name the calling API key in details. Some events record the entity concerned instead: the policy for policy_created and policy_updated, the list for custom_list_created, custom_list_updated, and custom_list_deleted, and the key acted on for api_key_* events. associated_object The id of the entity the action concerned (for example, the policy or user affected), when applicable. client_ip_address The address of the client whose request caused the event: the address of the connection or, for a request from a trusted proxy, the client address its X-Forwarded-For header names. It is recorded for every event a request causes, including a redaction completed later by the asynchronous worker, which records the address of the request that submitted the document. It is empty for an event with no request behind it, and never holds anything but an address. source Where the event came from: api for an event a request caused, or system for one Philter recorded on its own, such as at startup or when a session key expires in the background. details A short, non-sensitive description with extra context (for example, a role name or a counter), usually as key: value pairs separated by ,. A value supplied by a caller, such as a policy or context name, a hold reference, a document ID, a username, or a re-identification reason, is written in double quotes, escaped as a JSON string, when it is empty, begins or ends with a space, or contains ,, :, ", \, [, ], or a control, invisible formatting, private-use, or unassigned character, so it cannot be read as more than one field. Otherwise it is written as is. timestamp When the event occurred.

Audit events never contain the sensitive values themselves. For example, when a ledger is searched, the audit record stores a hash of the search term rather than the term; webhook configuration changes are recorded without the webhook URL or secret.

Writing an audit event can never fail the operation being audited: if the audit write fails, the failure is logged and the original operation still completes.

docs.title: What is audited
docs.text: The audit log focuses on actions that change state or affect security, plus authentication failures. The events Philter emits are grouped below.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Event When it is recorded api_authentication_failed A request was rejected because the API key was missing, malformed, or unknown. sign_in_succeeded A person signed in with a username and password. The subject is the user, the associated object is the session key issued, and the detail names the username and the key. Records the client IP address, never the password. sign_in_failed A sign-in was refused: a wrong password, an unknown username, a user without a password, or a deactivated user. The detail names the username that was tried, cut to 100 characters, with commas and control characters replaced by _. Records the client IP address, never the password. sign_in_locked Repeated failed sign-ins locked a username (lockout). The detail names the username, cut and cleaned as for sign_in_failed, the limit, and the lockout period. Records the client IP address. Recorded once per lock. A lock reached by wrong current passwords when changing a password or starting MFA enrollment also names the API key that made the request and the user. sign_in_unlocked An administrator cleared a user's sign-in lock with POST /api/users/{username}/sign-in/unlock. The subject is the administrator, the associated object is the user, and the detail names the calling API key. sign_in_rate_limited A client address went over the sign-in rate limit. The detail names the limit. Recorded for the first refused request in each minute, so a flood of requests is not a flood of events. admin_cross_user_access An admin read or acted on another user's resource via the owner parameter, or created an API key for a user who already had one (subject = the acting admin, associated object = the affected user), or listed every user's resources with all_users (subject = the acting admin, no associated object; the detail names the listing).

docs.title: Users
docs.text: Event When it is recorded user_created A user account was created. Created through the Users API, the subject is the calling administrator, the associated object is the new user, and the detail names the calling API key; for the admin user created at startup, the new user is both. user_email_changed A user's email address was set, changed, or removed through the Users API. The subject is the calling administrator, the associated object is the user, and the detail says whether the address was changed or removed and names the calling API key. The address itself is not recorded. user_role_changed A user's role was changed. Changed through the Users API, the subject is the calling administrator, the associated object is the user, and the detail names the calling API key. user_deactivated A user account was deactivated: API access is revoked, but the user record and all of its data are retained (the event detail records this). Deactivation never cascades, so governance evidence (the user's policies and redaction ledger) is preserved and stays resolvable to the retained user, and the account can be reactivated. user_reactivated A previously deactivated user account was reactivated, restoring API access. Through the Users API, deactivation and reactivation name the calling administrator as the subject and the calling API key in the detail. user_password_set A user without a password was given one, at creation or by an administrator through the Users API. The subject is the calling administrator, the associated object is the user, and the detail names the calling API key and whether a change is required. Never includes the password. user_password_reset An administrator replaced a user's password. Recorded like user_password_set. user_password_changed A user changed their own password. The subject and associated object are the user, and the detail names the calling API key. Never includes either password. user_mfa_enrolled A user confirmed TOTP MFA enrollment. The subject and associated object are the user, and the detail names the calling API key. Never includes the secret. user_mfa_removed A user's MFA enrollment was removed, by the user with a code or by an administrator, which also clears a lock. The subject is whoever removed it, and the detail names the calling API key. user_mfa_locked A user's MFA was locked after five consecutive bad codes. Recorded once per lock. user_mfa_unlocked An administrator unlocked a user's MFA. The subject is the administrator, and the detail names the calling API key.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text: Event When it is recorded api_key_created An API key was created. The subject is the key and the associated object is the user it belongs to. Created through the API Keys API, the detail names the user and the API key that asked for it. api_key_deleted An API key was deleted (soft-deleted): it is revoked and can no longer authenticate, but the key record is retained so audit entries that reference its id still resolve. Revoked through the API Keys API, the detail names the calling user and API key. api_key_scopes_changed An API key's scopes were changed. The entry records the scopes the key held before and after, so it shows whether the key was widened or narrowed. Changed through the API Keys API, the detail also names the calling user and API key. api_key_expired A session key passed its idle timeout or maximum lifetime and was revoked. The subject is the key, the associated object is its user, and the detail gives the reason. Recorded once, by whichever instance notices first: when a request presenting the key notices, the event records that request's address and the source api; otherwise, system.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text: Event When it is recorded policy_created A policy was created, through POST /api/policies or POST /api/policies/{name}/copy. policy_updated A policy was updated, through PUT /api/policies/{name}, or its description or notes through PUT /api/policies/{name}/details. When the description or notes changed, the details name them. policy_activated A policy was saved via the API and became active immediately. Recorded alongside policy_created or policy_updated, and attributing the change to the API key that made it. Details include the policy name. policy_deleted A policy was deleted. The associated object is the deleted policy; details include the policy name and where the deletion came from. policy_version_history_retrieved The version history of a policy was retrieved. Details include the policy name and the number of versions returned. policy_rolled_back A policy was rolled back to a prior revision. The associated object is the policy; details include the policy name, the target revision, and the new revision number.

docs.title: Contexts and custom lists
docs.text: Event When it is recorded contexts_retrieved The list of contexts was retrieved. context_created A context was created. context_deleted A context was deleted. context_updated A context's settings were changed with PATCH /api/contexts/{name}. The subject is the calling user, the associated object is the context, and the detail names the context, each setting that changed with its new value, and the calling API key. Sending a setting at its current value records nothing. context_entry_deleted A single context entry was deleted. context_entries_purged All entries were cleared from a context. context_entries_exported A context's mapping table was exported. context_entries_imported A mapping table was imported into a context. context_entries_export_denied An export was denied because the caller is not the context's creator or an admin (or the context does not exist). context_entries_import_denied An import was denied because the caller is not the context's creator or an admin (or the context does not exist). custom_lists_retrieved The list of custom lists was retrieved. custom_list_items_retrieved The items in a custom list were retrieved. custom_list_created A custom list was created. custom_list_updated A custom list was updated. custom_list_deleted A custom list was deleted.

docs.title: Documents and redaction
docs.text:
Event When it is recorded document_redaction_initiated A document was submitted for asynchronous redaction. document_redaction_completed A redaction completed. redacted_file_download A redacted document was downloaded. redacted_file_deleted An asynchronous redaction record was deleted. redaction_ledger_query The redaction ledger was queried or searched. redaction_ledger_deleted Ledger entries were deleted (by document or by retention). redaction_ledger_exported A ledger chain was exported, or an export was refused because an entry could not be read; the details then say count: 0, refused: entry_unreadable. redaction_reversed A cryptographic redaction was reversed via /api/reidentify or /api/reidentify/text. See Re-identification below.

For these events the details field carries extra context: document_redaction_initiated records the name and pinned version of the policy applied (along with the input and output content types), while document_redaction_completed records the number of redactions performed and the name and version of the policy that governed them.

docs.title: Re-identification
docs.text:
The redaction_reversed event is recorded every time /api/reidentify or /api/reidentify/text is called, regardless of whether individual values succeed or fail. Its details field records:

  • strategy: CRYPTO_REPLACE or FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE.
  • input: text, present only for /api/reidentify/text.
  • requested: the number of values submitted, or for a text, the number of tokens found in it.
  • succeeded: the number successfully decrypted.
  • reason: the caller's verbatim stated authority for the reversal, quoted as described for details when it contains a separator.
  • values: the list of encrypted input values (ciphertexts), in square brackets and separated by ,, each quoted the same way. For a text, these are the tokens found in it, without their braces. These are the replacement tokens, not the decrypted originals. The originals, and the text, are never written to the audit log.
  • owner: the target user id, present only when an admin used the owner parameter to act on behalf of another user.

This provides a full, auditable history of who un-redacted what, when, and under what stated authority. See Re-identification for the full endpoint documentation.

docs.title: Legal holds
docs.text:
Event When it is recorded legal_hold_set A legal hold was created. The details field includes the hold's reference, scope type, and scope value. legal_hold_released A legal hold was released. The details field includes the hold's reference and the id of the user who released it (releasedBy). legal_hold_blocked_deletion A deletion was blocked because one or more active holds cover the data. The details field lists the references of all blocking holds. This event is recorded on every blocked attempt: per-document delete, bulk purge, and age-based purge.

See Legal Holds for full documentation on the hold lifecycle and how holds block deletions.

docs.title: Output signing
docs.text:
Event When it is recorded signing_key_generated A new ES256 keypair was auto-generated on first start (no existing key was found in the database). signing_key_regenerated The signing key was regenerated through POST /api/signing-key/regenerate. Any consumer that cached the old public key will need to re-fetch the new one from GET /api/signing-key.

See Output Signing for the full documentation on key management and response verification.

docs.title: Account configuration
docs.text: Event When it is recorded redact_lists_retrieved The account's always-redact / never-redact lists were retrieved. redact_lists_updated The account's always-redact / never-redact lists were changed. webhook_configured A webhook URL and secret were configured. The details say whether a new secret was set (secret: set) or the existing one kept (secret: kept). The URL and secret are not recorded. Set through the API, the subject is the calling user and the detail names the calling API key. webhook_tested A test event was sent to the webhook. The details say whether the receiver accepted it and its status code, and name the calling API key. The URL and secret are not recorded. webhook_removed The webhook was removed. Removed through the API, the subject is the calling user and the detail names the calling API key. settings_updated An administrator changed the deployment settings. The details field names which settings changed (the webhook allowlist, output signing, or the Phield and Diffuse publishing settings) and never their values. Changed through the Settings API, the detail also names the calling API key.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Event When it is recorded storage_migrated Philter's data was copied from SQLite to MongoDB with the migrate-storage command, and every check of the copy passed. Recorded on the MongoDB side. The details field names the source file and how many records of each kind were copied. See Moving from SQLite to MongoDB. storage_guard_recovered With SQLite storage, Philter cleared a lock at startup that a Philter which stopped had left held: the queue admission lock, or an owner's evidence lock for legal-hold and ledger-deletion operations. The details field names the lock, the owner and operation for an evidence lock, and when it was taken. Review the operation it guarded, which may have been partly applied.

docs.title: Audit log access
docs.text: Event When it is recorded audit_log_retrieved The audit log was read through GET /api/audit. The details field records the filters applied and how many events matched. Reading the log is audited like any other access to evidence. audit_log_exported The audit log was exported as CSV through GET /api/audit/export. The details field records the date range, time zone, the offset or cursor the page started at, how many events were exported, whether the export was truncated, and the calling API key. pii_counts_retrieved The recorded PII counts were read through GET /api/pii-counts. The details field records the day range applied, the context when one was given (left out when the read covered every context), and how many entries matched.

docs.title: Exporting the audit log
docs.text:
Administrators can export the audit log as a CSV file with GET /api/audit/export. It requires an administrator and the audit:read scope.

  • Date range with a 30-day limit. from and to are required. to may be at most 30 days after from; a wider range, or a from after to, is refused.
  • Time zone. from and to are whole calendar days, read in the time zone given by the zone parameter, defaulting to the server's (the JVM default). The response reports the zone used. The to day is included in full, so the export covers from 00:00 up to, but not including, the start of the day after to, in that time zone.
  • Contents. The CSV has a header row followed by one row per event, newest first, with the columns timestamp, event, request_id, api_key_id, associated_object, client_ip_address, source, and details (the same fields described above; timestamps are written in ISO-8601, in UTC). As with the stored events, no sensitive values are included. A value beginning with =, +, -, @, a tab, or a carriage return is written with a leading apostrophe, so a spreadsheet shows it as text instead of running it as a formula. Most values are recorded by Philter itself, but some, such as a legal hold's reference, are written by callers.
  • Size. The API returns the range one page at a time: limit events per page (default 100, at most 1,000), with cursor and the X-Philter-Export-Next-Cursor header to fetch the next. Paging by cursor returns each event once even while events are recorded, including each page's own audit_log_exported event; see paging, including why offset paging of a range that includes the current day can repeat events.

docs.title: Reading the audit log over the API
docs.text: GET /api/audit returns audit events as JSON so the log can be shipped to a SIEM, pulled for a compliance review, or alerted on without a database connection. It requires an administrator and an API key holding the audit:read scope, and each read records an audit_log_retrieved event of its own. Each event it returns also carries username: the username of the user api_key_id names, when it names a user, including one since deactivated. It is resolved when the log is read, and absent when api_key_id names something other than a user, such as a policy or a key. See the Audit Log API for parameters and examples.

docs.title: Reviewing the audit log
docs.text:
The Audit Log API reads the audit log with either storage. The database can also be queried directly. With MongoDB, use standard MongoDB tooling; for example, to see the most recent events:

db.audit_events.find().sort({ timestamp: -1 }).limit(50)

To find all failed authentication attempts from a given IP address:

db.audit_events.find({ event: "api_authentication_failed", client_ip_address: "203.0.113.10" })

With SQLite, use the sqlite3 command line tool on the host that holds the database, as the user Philter runs as or as root (the Docker image does not include it). Here /srv/philter/data is the directory mounted at /opt/philter/data, and timestamps are milliseconds since the epoch:

sqlite3 /srv/philter/data/philter.db "SELECT datetime(timestamp / 1000, 'unixepoch'), event, details FROM audit_events ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50"

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Database
  • Redaction Ledgers for the separate, cryptographically-verifiable record of individual redactions.
  • API Keys and Authentication

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Philter caches several things to avoid repeated database lookups on the hot path:

  • API keys, so that authenticating a request does not query the database on every call.
  • Context entries (the token to replacement mappings used for consistent redaction within a context), so that repeated redactions in the same context reuse prior replacements quickly.
  • Sign-in counters: failed sign-ins per username, username locks, and sign-in requests per client address, used to lock and rate-limit password sign-in.

These use the shared cache backend described below. One additional cache is always kept in-process: the per-request policy and redact-list cache used by the filtering endpoints. It is never written to Valkey/Redis, because stored policies can contain PII in their filter-strategy conditions and the always/never redact terms are themselves sensitive. Each instance rebuilds it on a short TTL, so it needs no shared backend.

Philter supports two cache backends.

docs.title: In-memory cache (default)
docs.text:
When no cache host is configured, Philter uses a built-in, in-process cache. It requires no extra infrastructure and is the right choice for a single Philter instance. Because it lives inside the JVM, the cached data is ephemeral (it is lost on restart) and is not shared between instances. The Docker Compose configuration shipped with Philter runs this way, and Philter logs a warning at startup noting that the cache is in-memory.

Expired string entries and context hashes are reclaimed by a process-wide background task, with a one-second delay between cleanup passes, even if those keys are never read again. Reads also reject expired values immediately. Closing an individual cache wrapper does not stop cleanup for other users of the shared store.

The in-memory backend bounds live and non-expiring entries by entry count and accounted bytes. At capacity, writes become cache misses. See the capacity settings below.

docs.title: Valkey/Redis cache (distributed deployments)
docs.text:
CACHE_HOSTNAME is required when more than one Philter instance shares a database: every instance must use the same Valkey/Redis, and running several instances without one is not a supported deployment. Without a shared cache, each instance keeps its own in-process cache, so an API key revoked on one instance would remain valid in another instance's cache until that entry expires (API_KEY_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS), and the per-address sign-in rate limit would be counted per instance. A single instance needs no shared cache.

Newly created context replacements are not in this list, because consistency there is enforced in the database by a unique constraint on the token, an atomic insert, and concurrent writers being handed the stored winner, and because a cache miss reads the database, so instances agree on a replacement whatever their caches hold. Separate caches lower the fleet-wide hit rate and add database traffic rather than changing the answer.

Invalidation is the part that does need a shared cache. When a mapping is overwritten by an import or deleted, Philter forgets it in the cache it can reach, which is every instance's when they share one and only the local one when they do not. Note that eviction does not make a change instantaneous even with a shared cache: a reader that loaded the old value just before the write can still store it again afterwards.

Pointing every instance at the same Valkey (or Redis) server gives a durable, shared cache that resolves both the stale-key and the invalidation problems.

docs.title: Horizontal scaling
docs.text: API requests (/api/**) are stateless: each one is authenticated from its own API key and depends on no server-side session, so any instance can serve any request and you can run as many instances as you need behind a plain load balancer. The shared cache above is what keeps those instances consistent.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set the following environment variables on each Philter instance. When CACHE_HOSTNAME is unset or blank, Philter falls back to the in-memory cache.

Variable Required Default Description CACHE_HOSTNAME Yes, to enable Valkey/Redis (unset, uses in-memory) Hostname of the Valkey/Redis server. CACHE_PORT No 6379 Port of the Valkey/Redis server. CACHE_PASSWORD No (none) Password, if the server requires authentication. CACHE_SSL No false Set to true to connect over TLS.

docs.title: Protecting the cache
docs.text:
Treat Valkey like the database. Philter encrypts what it stores there, but anything that can reach the server can still delete entries, which costs only a database read, and can see how much is cached and when.

  • Values are encrypted and authenticated. Each value is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and bound to the name it is stored under. A value that was not written by Philter, was copied from another entry, or was written back after it expired reads as absent, so Philter goes to the database instead. This is designed so that something able to write to Valkey cannot make Philter accept an API key it did not issue, or change the replacements written into redacted output.
  • Names are hashed. Key and field names are replaced by keyed hashes, so the cache does not show user IDs, context names, or API key hashes.
  • Not covered: the sign-in counters (requests per client address, and failures for usernames with no account), which Valkey increments itself and so are stored as plain numbers under hashed names. Changing them can only weaken those limits; the lockout of an existing account is kept in the database. A context replacement removed from the cache can be written back and is accepted until the expiry sealed inside it, an hour after it was cached; it is still a replacement Philter issued for that same value. Likewise, a cached API key record removed when the key was revoked or its scopes narrowed can be written back and is accepted until its sealed expiry, at most API_KEY_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS after it was cached, so the key keeps working, or regains its earlier scopes, for that long. A deactivated user's keys and an expired or revoked session key are still refused, since both are checked against the database on every request. Lower API_KEY_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS to shorten this window.

Every instance sharing a cache must use the same PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, as they must for a shared database. When the key changes, entries written under the old key read as absent and are replaced as they are used. Each instance logs one warning the first time it finds an entry it cannot decrypt.

When CACHE_HOSTNAME names a host other than this machine and CACHE_PASSWORD is empty or CACHE_SSL is false, Philter logs a warning at startup. Set a password, use TLS unless the cache is reachable only on a private network, and allow only Philter's instances to connect.

docs.title: Cache lifetimes (TTL)
docs.text:
Two caches keep entries for a short, configurable time. Both default to a low value so stale data is short-lived; raise them to trade freshness for fewer database reads.

Variable Default Description API_KEY_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS 60 How long a resolved API key is cached. Revoking a key through the API evicts it from the cache immediately; this TTL bounds how long a key revoked out-of-band (for example, edited directly in the database) keeps working. REDACTION_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS 60 How long the filtering endpoints keep a user's policy and always/never redact lists in-process. A cached copy is used only while its revisions match the stored ones, checked on every request, so an edited or deleted policy or list applies to the next request on every instance, with or without a shared cache; this setting bounds memory, not staleness. This cache is always in-process and is never written to Valkey/Redis.

docs.title: Docker Compose example
docs.text:
The bundled docker-compose.yml uses the in-memory cache. To add a shared cache, add a Valkey service with a password and set CACHE_HOSTNAME and CACHE_PASSWORD on the philter service to point at it. Valkey is reachable only on the Compose network here, so this example does not use TLS, and Philter logs the warning described in Protecting the cache:

  philter:
    # ...existing configuration...
    environment:
      CACHE_HOSTNAME: valkey
      CACHE_PORT: 6379
      CACHE_PASSWORD: ${CACHE_PASSWORD:?set CACHE_PASSWORD}
      CACHE_SSL: false
      # ...existing environment...
    depends_on:
      # ...existing dependencies...
      valkey:
        condition: service_healthy

  valkey:
    image: valkey/valkey:latest
    networks:
      - philter
    environment:
      CACHE_PASSWORD: ${CACHE_PASSWORD:?set CACHE_PASSWORD}
    command: ["sh", "-c", "exec valkey-server --save 60 1 --loglevel warning --requirepass \"$$CACHE_PASSWORD\""]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -a \"$$CACHE_PASSWORD\" ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

The in-memory backend bounds both entry count (including every hash field) and accounted retained bytes. Defaults are 100,000 entries and 64 MiB; configure IN_MEMORY_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES and IN_MEMORY_CACHE_MAX_BYTES with positive values. A full store makes room rather than refusing: it drops expired entries, then those nearest to expiring, so a heavy user lowers the hit rate instead of stopping caching. Sign-in counts are kept in a separate store with the same bounds, so no amount of cached data can push them out. Increasing capacity does not make the in-memory backend suitable for multiple instances; those still require a shared cache.

docs.title: Context mapping freshness
docs.text: Every cached mapping has a fixed maximum age of 3,600 seconds, measured from the start of the database observation that populated it. Reads reject expired mappings even if unrelated writes keep the containing context hash alive. A delayed cache fill cannot restart that age. This bounds stale mappings after import/deletion or a concurrent fill; it does not provide immediate consistency after mutation. The bound assumes reasonably synchronized instance clocks.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Philter stores everything it persists in a SQLite file by default, for a single Philter instance with no database server, or in a MongoDB database, which several instances can share. Choose with STORAGE_TYPE (sqlite or mongodb); see Settings. Philter does not start without its storage. The same data is stored either way: this page describes it with MongoDB's collection names, which SQLite's tables share, and SQLite describes how SQLite storage differs.

docs.title: Choosing SQLite or MongoDB
docs.text:
Choose the storage with STORAGE_TYPE before Philter's first start. A deployment that starts on SQLite can later move its data to MongoDB with the migrate-storage command (see Moving from SQLite to MongoDB); Philter does not move data from MongoDB to SQLite.

SQLite (STORAGE_TYPE=sqlite, the default) MongoDB (STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb) Philter instances One. A second Philter on the same file refuses to start. Any number, sharing one database, for high availability. What to run Nothing: the database is a file Philter creates, at SQLITE_PATH. A MongoDB server, replica set, or managed service such as Atlas, at MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING. Suits Evaluations, small single-server deployments, edge devices, air-gapped hosts, and the cloud marketplace images. Production deployments that need more than one instance, or that already run MongoDB. Backups The database file, copied with SQLite's online backup. MongoDB's own backup tools. Bundled Compose file docker-compose.yml docker-compose.mongodb.yml Philter Diffuse Cannot read the PII counts yet; read them through the PII Counts API. Reads the PII counts from MongoDB.

Both keep the same data, encrypt the same fields with PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, record a schema version, and never expire the redaction ledger, audit log, or legal holds on their own. Settings are in Database Settings. The sections below describe MongoDB, then SQLite describes how SQLite storage differs.

A deployment that sets MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING must also set STORAGE_TYPE. Philter refuses to start otherwise, so a deployment that used MongoDB, as Philter 3 always did, does not start on a new, empty SQLite database.

docs.title: Supported MongoDB versions
docs.text: Philter is developed and tested against MongoDB 8.2, which is what the bundled docker-compose.mongodb.yml pins (./compose.sh -f docker-compose.mongodb.yml up). That MongoDB requires authentication and holds the ledger, the audit log and the encrypted PII. Its port is not published, so only Philter, on the compose network, can reach it. To use mongosh or Philter Diffuse from your machine, add ports: ["127.0.0.1:27017:27017"] to the mongodb service. Its development password is written in docker-compose.mongodb.yml; for real data, use a generated password. SQLite storage uses the SQLite library built into Philter; there is nothing to install.

docs.title: What Philter stores
docs.text:
Data Description Users User accounts, roles, webhook settings, and optional bcrypt password hashes. API keys Hashed API keys and their metadata. Policies Redaction policies, including the managed policies shipped with Philter. Contexts and context entries Contexts and their token-to-replacement mappings used for referential integrity. Custom lists Named term lists referenced by policies. Always/never redact lists Per-account always-redact / never-redact term lists. Pending documents Records for asynchronous PDF redactions, including encrypted input/output, attempt tokens, renewable computation leases, and publication reservations. Finished records have a TTL; interrupted publication requires operator recovery. Webhook deliveries Delivery records for outbound webhook notifications (subject to a TTL). Schema version The schema_version collection: the version of the data layout, when each migration ran, and the lock an instance holds while migrating. Evidence operation coordination The evidence_operation_guards collection serializes hold changes and ledger deletions per owner. Guards do not expire; interrupted operations require the recovery procedure in Legal Holds. Administrator change coordination The administrator_change_guard collection lets one change at a time, across instances, demote or deactivate an administrator, so concurrent changes cannot remove the last active administrator. A guard left by an instance that stopped is free again after 30 seconds. Active signing key The signing_key_state collection contains the single active-key pointer. Key history remains in signing_keys so earlier signatures can be verified after rotation. Ledger chain lifecycle The ledger_chains collection tracks open, writing, failed, completed, and purged chains. Purged markers prevent late appends; they contain owner/document IDs and lifecycle timestamps, not tokens or replacements. Redaction ledger The cryptographic ledger of redactions, when enabled for a context. See Redaction Ledgers. Disambiguation vectors The vectors collection: per-(user, context) vector hashes learned for span disambiguation, bounded by MAX_VECTORS_PER_CONTEXT. Sign-in challenges The sign_in_challenges collection: short-lived, single-use MFA sign-in challenges, stored as a hash and expired by a TTL index. Admin settings Instance-wide administrator settings, such as output signing and Phield publishing. See the Settings API. Audit events The audit log of security-relevant actions. See Auditing.

Some collections are encrypted at rest and some are not. See What is encrypted at rest below and encryption.

docs.title: What is encrypted at rest
docs.text:
Encryption is per collection, not blanket. Each encrypted record carries its own random data key, stored wrapped under PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so the master key is required to read any of it.

Encrypted:

Collection What is protected users Account details and the webhook secret ledger The original token and its replacement policies The policy, its description, and its notes policy_versions Each revision of a policy policy_contents Policy content, by its SHA-256 hash; the hash stays readable, since redaction evidence names it custom_lists List items redact_lists Always/never redact terms webhook_deliveries The queued webhook signing secret; delivery metadata and payload remain readable pending_documents The submitted document, the redacted result, and the resolved configuration captured for the job signing_keys The private half of the signing keypair (the public half stays readable, since verifiers need it) admin_settings The Phield API key

What Philter stores in a Valkey cache is encrypted under PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY too, and its key names are hashed.

The audit log is deliberately readable: it is evidence of who did what, and encrypting it would make it unusable for the reporting it exists for. It records event names, the acting API key, an object id, a client address and a short detail string, not document content.

Not encrypted: API keys (stored as a hash), context entries (stored as a token hash, not the original value), policy names, contexts, legal holds, disambiguation vectors (vectors, hashes only), sign-in challenges (stored as a hash), the rest of the admin settings, webhook delivery metadata and payloads, a pending document's submitting client address (recorded on its audit events, which hold it in the clear too), and the audit log. These hold no recoverable secret.

File names are stored in the clear. The file name sent with a redaction (the filename parameter) is kept readable on its ledger chain and on its asynchronous job, so the Ledger and Documents APIs can search and sort by it. An asynchronous job's webhook payload also carries it, and queued delivery payloads are stored readably. Do not put sensitive values, such as a person's name, in file names; use an identifier instead.

A key written into a policy can be read by anyone who can read the policy. The crypto and fpe sections of a policy may contain an encryption key. Policies are encrypted at rest, but the policy's owner, and an administrator when ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED is on, can read the policy and the key in it, and reverse what that key encrypted. Prefix the value with env: (for example env:CRYPTO_KEY) to keep the key in the environment and store only the variable's name; the variable must be listed in POLICY_ALLOWED_ENV_KEYS. Philter logs a warning when a policy is saved with a key in it. Note that a version snapshot keeps whatever the policy held at the time, so changing an existing policy to use env: does not remove the old key from its history.

docs.title: Configuring the MongoDB connection
docs.text:
With STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb, Philter connects to MongoDB using a standard MongoDB connection string, set with the MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING environment variable.

Environment Variable Description Default Value MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING The MongoDB connection string Philter uses to connect to the database. mongodb://localhost:27017

Philter always uses the database named philter. A database name in the connection string does not change it; there it only serves as the default authentication database when authSource is not set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A local, unauthenticated MongoDB (the default):

MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb://localhost:27017

A MongoDB that requires authentication:

MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb://philter_user:your-password@db-host:27017/philter?authSource=admin

A replica set (recommended for production, so the database is not a single point of failure):

MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb://user:pass@host1:27017,host2:27017,host3:27017/philter?replicaSet=rs0&authSource=admin

MongoDB Atlas or another mongodb+srv host:

MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb+srv://user:pass@cluster0.example.mongodb.net/philter?retryWrites=true&w=majority

Philter launched from a cloud marketplace image uses SQLite storage, with its database on the virtual machine's disk, and runs no MongoDB. To have it use MongoDB instead, for example an external or managed database, set STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb and MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING before putting data in it.

docs.title: MongoDB indexes
docs.text:
With MongoDB, Philter creates the indexes it needs automatically at startup. Each data service ensures its own indexes when it initializes, and index creation in MongoDB is idempotent, so this is safe on every restart and adds no manual setup. The indexes cover the access patterns Philter uses, for example:

  • api_keys by api_key_hash (the authentication lookup) and by user.
  • policies, contexts, custom_lists, and redact_lists by user (and name where applicable).
  • context_entries by (user_id, context_name, token_hash) for the redaction hot path.
  • ledger by chain head and by document for each user, and by chain head across users.
  • pending_documents by status and by document, with a TTL index that expires finished records (PENDING_DOCUMENTS_TTL_SECONDS, default 7 days).
  • webhook_deliveries by delivery status, with a TTL index (WEBHOOK_DELIVERIES_TTL_SECONDS, default 30 days).
  • users by username, and audit_events by timestamp, by timestamp and _id (for paging the CSV export), and by event.

Required uniqueness and retention indexes must be created and their options verified; a failure prevents startup. Incompatible TTL settings also fail startup. Only optional performance-index failures are logged and tolerated. Ledger collections must have no automatic TTL index, regardless of its name. Philter rejects incompatible indexes without dropping them. Provision the required schema and privileges before starting the application.

docs.title: Schema version and migrations
docs.text:
Philter records the version of its data layout in schema_version in its database, a collection with MongoDB and a table with SQLite, and checks it each time it starts, before it serves any request:

  • A new database is recorded at the version the running Philter expects.
  • An older version is brought up to date: Philter runs each pending migration in order and records each one, with when it ran, as it completes. A database that holds data but no recorded version was written before versions were recorded and is migrated from the first version.
  • A newer version, written by a newer Philter, stops Philter from starting with a message naming both versions. Philter does not change the data. Run the newer release, or restore a backup taken before it ran.
  • A failed migration stops Philter from starting. The log names the migration and why it failed, and the recorded version stays at the last migration that completed, so a release with a fix continues from there.

When several instances start together, as they can with MongoDB, one takes a lock and migrates while the others wait for it, up to SCHEMA_MIGRATION_WAIT_SECONDS (see Settings). The lock expires if the instance holding it stops, so another can take over. Each start logs the version it found and each migration it ran.

Migrations change data in place. Back up the database before upgrading Philter; see Upgrading.

docs.title: MongoDB operational notes
docs.text:
• Backups. MongoDB holds your policies, contexts, ledger, and audit log. Back it up like any other production datastore, and before every upgrade, since an upgrade may migrate the data.
  • Network access. Restrict network access to the database to the Philter instances that need it.
  • Multiple Philter instances. When running more than one Philter instance, point them all at the same MongoDB so they share state. They should also share a cache; see Caching.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite storage, the default (STORAGE_TYPE=sqlite), keeps all of Philter's data in one SQLite file, named by SQLITE_PATH, with no database server to run. It suits evaluations, small single-server deployments, edge devices, and air-gapped hosts. Everything above about what is stored and what is encrypted at rest applies to it too: the same data is kept, the same fields are encrypted with the same PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and the redaction ledger, audit log, and legal holds never expire on their own.

One Philter instance only. SQLite storage supports exactly one Philter process per database file. While it runs, Philter holds an exclusive lock on a file beside the database (SQLITE_PATH with .lock appended), and a second Philter started against the same database refuses to start. Several instances behind a load balancer, as in High Availability, need MongoDB. Do not put the database on a network file system: SQLite's locking is not reliable there.

The files. Philter creates the database file at first start, along with SQLite's write-ahead log files beside it (-wal and -shm). Keep them together, on local disk, in a directory only Philter's user can read. Philter creates these files readable and writable only by the user it runs as, and narrows an existing database file that other users could read when it starts. The Docker image's data directory is readable only by its philter user. The Docker image keeps the database at /opt/philter/data/philter.db; mount a volume at /opt/philter/data, as the bundled docker-compose.yml does, or the data is lost when the container is removed.

Schema. At first start Philter creates the tables of the current schema version, and later releases migrate them at startup as they do for MongoDB.

Locks left by a stop. If Philter stops part way through an asynchronous submission or a legal-hold or ledger-deletion operation, the lock that operation held stays held. With SQLite, Philter clears such locks when it next starts, since no other Philter can be using the database, and records each one in the audit log as storage_guard_recovered. See Legal Holds.

Expiry. Instead of TTL indexes, finished asynchronous documents, finished webhook deliveries, and sign-in challenges are deleted once they are past their retention, by a check that runs every minute and as Philter writes new ones. An expired sign-in challenge or session key is refused whether or not it has been deleted yet.

Backups. SQLite's online backup is consistent while Philter runs. Run it with the sqlite3 command line tool on the host that holds the database, as the user Philter runs as or as root, for example sqlite3 /srv/philter/data/philter.db ".backup '/backups/philter.db'" where /srv/philter/data is the directory mounted at /opt/philter/data. The Docker image does not include sqlite3. Otherwise, stop Philter and copy the database file together with its -wal and -shm files; copying the database file alone while Philter runs can miss writes still in the -wal file. Back up PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY separately: the encrypted data in a backup cannot be read without it.

A backup holds everything the database does, including password hashes and the audit log, and a copy made with sqlite3 or cp gets the permissions your umask gives new files, not the database's. Keep backups where only the people who administer Philter can read them, for example with umask 077 before making the copy, or chmod 600 on the backup file and chmod 700 on its directory.

Changing storage. A deployment that outgrows one instance can move its SQLite database to MongoDB; see Moving from SQLite to MongoDB. Philter does not move data from MongoDB to SQLite. A deployment that sets MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING must also set STORAGE_TYPE; Philter refuses to start otherwise, so a deployment that used MongoDB does not start on a new, empty SQLite database.

docs.title: Moving from SQLite to MongoDB
docs.text:
A deployment that starts on SQLite and later needs several Philter instances behind a load balancer, as in High Availability, moves its data to MongoDB with the migrate-storage command. It copies everything SQLite storage holds into an empty MongoDB database: users with their password hashes and MFA, API keys, policies with their version history, custom and redact lists, contexts with their mappings, legal holds, the redaction ledger, the signing keys, asynchronous documents and webhook deliveries, PII counts, and the audit log.

Records are copied as stored. Every record keeps its id, timestamps, revisions, and state; ledger entries keep their hashes and signatures, so chains signed before the move still verify after it; encrypted fields are copied without being decrypted, so the same PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY reads them on MongoDB. Nothing is re-audited or re-signed.

  1. Stop Philter. The command refuses to run while a Philter is using the SQLite database.
  2. Back up the SQLite database (see Backups). The command opens it read-only and does not change it, but keep the backup until Philter is running on MongoDB.

  3. Run the command with the SQLite database, an empty MongoDB database, and the encryption key:

    SQLITE_PATH=/opt/philter/data/philter.db \
MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb://... \
PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY=... \
java -jar philter.jar migrate-storage --to mongodb

    With Docker, run the image with the data volume mounted, the same variables, and the command in place of the image's own (Docker Compose prefixes the bundled docker-compose.yml's philter-data volume with the project name; docker volume ls shows the full name):

    docker run --rm -v philter-data:/opt/philter/data \
    -e MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING=mongodb://... -e PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY=... \
    philterd/philter java -jar /opt/philter/philter.jar migrate-storage --to mongodb
    4. Start Philter with STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb, the same MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING, and the same PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Keep the SQLite database until you have confirmed Philter works on MongoDB; going back means starting Philter on it again with STORAGE_TYPE=sqlite.

The command refuses, writing nothing to MongoDB, when the MongoDB database already holds Philter data (it never merges), when the SQLite database is not at the schema version this Philter expects (start this release on it once, stop it, and migrate), when a Philter is using the SQLite database, or when a Philter stopped part way through an operation and left a lock held in it (start Philter on it once with STORAGE_TYPE=sqlite, which clears the lock and records that in the audit log, stop it, and migrate).

After copying, it checks the copy: the number of records of each kind, every ledger chain's hashes and signatures, the active signing key and every retained public key, and a sample of each kind of encrypted field, decrypted with PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY. It prints how many records of each kind it copied, and exits with status 0 only when every check passes. When a check fails, it says what did not match and exits with status 1; do not start Philter on that MongoDB database. Drop its philter database, fix the cause (most often a different PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, or a ledger chain that did not validate in SQLite either), and run the command again. A successful migration is recorded in the audit log on MongoDB as storage_migrated, with the source file and the counts copied.

Not copied: the schema version history, which MongoDB records afresh at the version copied, and locks held by operations in progress, which hold nothing once Philter has stopped.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Settings for the full list of configuration environment variables.
  • System Requirements.
  • Caching for the optional shared cache.

Policy JSON is retained in policy_contents by SHA-256, independently of immutable owner/name/revision references in policy_versions. policy_revision_counters retains revision allocation across live policy deletion and name reuse. Failed or competing attempts can leave revision gaps and retained candidate snapshots; the live policy identifies the published head. Explicit queued policy pins fail if their content is missing or does not match its fingerprint.

docs.title: Async coordination and retention
docs.text: pending_documents uses retention_at for TTL, set only after durable notification intent is acknowledged. webhook_deliveries uses terminal completed_at for both success and failure. Unexpected TTL fields prevent startup. A job's resolved configuration is stored only on its pending_documents record and expires or is deleted with it. queue_admission serializes capacity checks and insertion across instances; ambiguous operations retain the guard for operator recovery. queue_scheduling retains per-account/global scheduling rounds for fair claims. A job's optional fairness_key orders an account's own jobs among its rounds and is stored unencrypted. No legacy migration or backfill is performed.

docs.title: De-identification Methods
docs.text:
There are several ways data can be de-identified, and which you use depends on the types of data you want to de-identify and your use-case for de-identifying the data. The terminology around the different methods is often used interchangeably, but there are differences between each method.

In this User's Guide, we may use the terms filter and redact interchangeably.

In Philter, de-identification methods vary for each type of sensitive information. For example, all types can be replaced or redacted, but only dates can be shifted and only zip codes can be truncated. How a de-identification method is applied by Philter is called a filter strategy. Each type of sensitive information can have one or more filter strategies, and the combination of the filter strategies you select is called a policy. A policy determines how a document will be de-identified.

The following is a list of de-identification methods that describes how each method works and its applicability to Philter. Deidentifying a document is likely to require a combination of the following methods. For instance, you may want to redact names, encrypt credit card numbers, and shift appointment dates.

docs.title: Summary of Deidentification Methods
docs.text:
De-identification MethodDescriptionReplacementReplaces sensitive information with a defined value. For example, you might want to replace a credit card number with the literal value "CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER".Redaction and MaskingRemoves sensitive information. Philter gives you a choice of how to remove the sensitive information, whether it is by replacing it with ***** (masking) or by some other set of characters.EncryptionEncrypts sensitive information.Date ShiftingShifts dates either forward or backward by some interval.BucketingCategorizes data into buckets based on the data. Examples of bucketing is Philter can bucket dates into years, and zip codes by population.

A difference between Philter and other services is that Philter does not send your data to a third party for de-identification. Philter runs in your cloud and your data stays in your cloud.

docs.title: Redaction and Masking
docs.text:
Redaction and masking are two methods of de-identification that are often used interchangeably. The term redaction refers to removing a sensitive value from a document. When we hear the term redaction we often think of an image of a document with black bars across pieces of the text.

Masking is similar to redaction but allows for configuring how the sensitive value is removed. The most common example is using asterisks (i.e. ******) in place of a sensitive value.

docs.title: Replacement
docs.text:
Replacement is a method of de-identification that simply replaces a sensitive value with another value. Replacement is useful when the sensitive value is not needed once the document has been de-identified. Philter can replace a sensitive value with a preset value or with a random value.

In Philter's filter strategies, replacement is achieved by using the strategy to REDACT, STATIC_REPLACE , or RANDOM_REPLACE .

docs.title: Bucketing
docs.text:
Bucketing is a method of de-identification that categorizes data into buckets based on the data. Bucketing is useful when the exact value is not needed, but the general category is important for analysis.

In Philter, bucketing can be applied to several types of data. For example:

  • Zip Codes: Zip codes can be bucketed by their population. This allows for redacting zip codes with a population below a certain threshold.
  • Dates: Dates can be bucketed into years or other time intervals.

docs.title: Date Shifting
docs.text:
Date shifting is a method of de-identification that shifts dates either forward or backward by some interval. Date shifting is useful when the exact date is sensitive, but the relationship between dates in a document or set of documents is important to preserve.

In Philter, date shifting is achieved by using the SHIFT or SHIFTRANDOM filter strategies. These strategies allow you to specify the number of days, minutes, months, and years to shift the date.

Option Description shiftDays The number of days to shift the date. Can be a negative or positive integer. shiftMinutes The number of minutes to shift the date. Can be a negative or positive integer. shiftMonths The number of months to shift the date. Can be a negative or positive integer. shiftYears The number of years to shift the date. Can be a negative or positive integer.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Encryption is a method of de-identification that replaces a sensitive value with its encrypted version. Encryption is useful when the sensitive value may need to be recovered later by an authorized party.

Philter provides two primary methods of encryption:

  • AES Encryption: Using the CRYPTO_REPLACE filter strategy, Philter encrypts the sensitive value using AES in GCM mode (authenticated encryption). This requires an encryption key to be defined in the policy.
  • Format Preserving Encryption (FPE): Using the FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE filter strategy, Philter encrypts the sensitive value while preserving its original format (e.g., an encrypted credit card number will still look like a credit card number).

docs.title: Differential-Privacy Reporting with Philter Diffuse
docs.text:
Philter Diffuse applies differential privacy (using OpenDP) to aggregate PII counts, producing compliance-ready reports with a tracked privacy budget. Philter can optionally record the PII type counts from its redactions so that Diffuse can privatize and report on them.

When this is enabled, after each redaction Philter records counts only, never any PII.

docs.title: What Philter records
docs.text:
Philter writes aggregated, time-bucketed document-presence counts to pii_count_aggregates in its database, one record per user's (context, day). As MongoDB stores it:

{
  "user_id": ObjectId("6a0f1c2e9b1d4e3f2a1b0c9d"),
  "context": "claims-intake",
  "bucket_start": ISODate("2026-05-31T00:00:00Z"),
  "counts": { "ssn": 1240, "email-address": 8900, "person": 9500 },
  "total_documents": 10000,
  "updated_at": ISODate("2026-05-31T18:42:10Z")
}

For each redaction that finds PII, every distinct PII type present increments that type's counter by one, and total_documents increments by one. A redaction that finds no PII is not recorded, so total_documents counts documents that contained PII, not all documents redacted. counts.ssn is the number of documents in that day's bucket (for that context) that contained at least one SSN.

This "document-presence" counting is deliberate: it ensures each redaction contributes at most one to any count, which preserves the sensitivity = 1 assumption that Diffuse's differential-privacy guarantee depends on. (Counting the total number of SSN spans instead would let a single document contribute many, which would weaken the privacy guarantee Diffuse reports.)

Because the counts are bucketed per user's (context, day), the collection stays small regardless of redaction volume, so no retention TTL is required.

docs.title: Reading the counts through the API
docs.text:
The PII Counts API (GET /api/pii-counts) returns the same counts with an API key, so a reader needs no access to Philter's database and does not depend on how Philter stores them. Each entry gives an id, a UTC day, the count for each PII type, and totalDocuments, and the context and its owner when the reader may see them. Narrow it by day range and context, and page through it with offset and limit. It requires an administrator and the pii-counts:read scope, and each read is recorded in the audit log.

curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  "https://localhost:8080/api/pii-counts?from=2026-09-01&to=2026-09-30"

The response's recordingEnabled field says whether Philter is recording counts now, so an empty result can be told apart from recording being off.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
Recording is controlled by a single global admin setting and is off by default (data minimization: statistics are not collected unless you opt in). An administrator enables it with the Settings API ({"diffuseCountsEnabled": true}).

Recording is best-effort: any failure is ignored so it can never affect redaction, and when the setting is off there is no per-redaction overhead.

docs.title: Producing a report
docs.text:
Philter Diffuse reads the recorded counts through the PII Counts API, so it needs only a Philter API key: no access to Philter's database, and it works with either storage type. The key must hold the pii-counts:read scope and belong to an administrator. Put it in the PHILTER_API_KEY environment variable and pass Philter's URL with --philter-url:

export PHILTER_API_KEY=<api key>
python main.py --philter-url https://localhost:8080 --aggregates --output privatized_counts.csv

Add --context <name> to restrict the report to a single context, and --from and --to (UTC days, YYYY-MM-DD) to restrict it to a range of days. If recording is turned off, Diffuse says so and writes no report. With the self-signed certificate the Docker image generates, pass that certificate to Diffuse with --philter-ca-cert (see TLS). Diffuse adds calibrated noise, tracks the epsilon (privacy loss) budget, and writes privatized counts. See the Philter Diffuse documentation for the privacy budget, scale/epsilon options, and report formats.

Diffuse can still read the pii_count_aggregates collection directly from Philter's MongoDB (--mongo-uri "mongodb://localhost:27017/philter" --aggregates, with STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb), but that path is deprecated in Philter Diffuse and will be removed.

docs.title: How to Evaluate Philter's Performance
docs.text:
A common question we receive is how well does Philter perform? Our answer to this question is probably less than satisfactory because it simply depends. What does it depend on? Philter's performance is heavily dependent upon your individual data. Sharing to compare metrics of Philter's performance between different customer datasets is like comparing apples and oranges.

If your data is not exactly like another customer's data then the metrics will not be applicable to your data. In terms of the classic information retrieval metrics precision and recall, comparing these values between customers can give false impressions about Philter's performance, both good and bad.

This guide walks you through how to evaluate Philter's performance. If you are just getting started with Philter please see the Quick Starts instead. Then you can come back here to learn how to evaluate Philter'ss performance.

docs.title: Guide to Evaluating Performance
docs.text: We have created this guide to help guide you in evaluating Philter's performance on your data. The guide involves determining the types of sensitive information you want to redact, configuring those filters, optimizing the configuration, and then capturing the performance metrics.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
To evaluate Philter's performance you need:

  • An application using Philter.
  • A list of the types of sensitive information you want to redact.
  • A data set representative of the text you will be redacting using Philter. It's important the data set be representative so the evaluation results will transfer to the actual data redaction.
  • The same data set but with annotated sensitive information. These annotations will be used to calculate the precision and recall metrics.

docs.title: Configuring Philter
docs.text: Before we can begin our evaluation we need to create a policy. A policy is a configuration that defines the types of sensitive information that will be redacted and how it will be redacted. Policies are stored in a database and are managed with the Policies API.

docs.title: Creating a Policy
docs.text:
Write a new policy, or copy the default policy with POST /api/policies/default/copy?name=... and modify the copy for your needs.

When creating a new policy, the configuration will be similar to what's shown below:

{
   "identifiers": {
      "emailAddress": {
         "emailAddressFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      },
      "phoneNumber": {
         "phoneNumberFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      }
   }
}

A policy's name is not part of its JSON: it is the name query parameter of POST /api/policies. This walkthrough names the policy evaluation.

docs.title: Identifying the Filters You Need
docs.text: The policy contains the filters that are enabled. We need to make sure that each type of sensitive information that you want to redact is represented by a filter in the policy. Look through the policy and determine which filters are listed that you do not need and also which filters you do need that are not listed.

docs.title: Disabling Filters We Do Not Need
docs.text: If a filter is listed in the policy, and you do not need the filter you have two options. You can either remove the filter from the policy, or you can set the filter's enabled property to false. Using the enabled property allows you to keep the filter configuration in the policy in case it is needed later but both options have the same effect.

docs.title: Enabling Filters Not in the Default Policy
docs.text:
Let's say you want to redact bitcoin addresses. The bitcoin address filter is not in the default policy. To add the bitcoin address filter we will refer to Philter's documentation on the bitcoin address filter, get the configuration, and copy it into the policy.

From the bitcoin address filter documentation we see the configuration for the bitcoin address filter is:

      "bitcoinAddress": {
         "bitcoinFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      }

We can copy this configuration and paste it into our policy:

{
   "identifiers": {
      "bitcoinAddress": {
         "bitcoinFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      },
      "emailAddress": {
         "emailAddressFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      },
      "phoneNumber": {
         "phoneNumberFilterStrategies": [
            {
               "strategy": "REDACT",
               "redactionFormat": "{{{REDACTED-%t}}}"
            }
         ]
      }
   }
}

The order of the filters in the policy does not matter and has no impact on performance. We typically place the filters in the policy alphabetically just to improve readability.

Repeat these steps until you have added a filter for each of the types of sensitive information you want to redact. Typically, the default redaction strategy and redactionFormat values for each filter should be fine for evaluation.

When finished modifying the policy, create it with POST /api/policies?name=evaluation, or, if it already exists (such as a copy of the default policy), replace it with PUT /api/policies/{policyName}. There is no need to restart Philter; the policy will be available immediately for use.

docs.title: Submitting Text for Redaction
docs.text:
With our policy in place we can now send text to Philter for redaction using that policy:

curl -k -X POST "https://localhost:8080/api/filter?p=evaluation" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  --data-binary @document.txt

The explain API endpoint produces a detailed description of the redaction. The response will include a list of spans that contain the start and stop positions of redacted text and the type of sensitive information that was redacted. Using this information we can compare the redacted information to our annotated file to calculate precision and recall metrics.

docs.title: Calculating Precision and Recall
docs.text:
Now we can calculate the precision and recall metrics.

  • Precision is the number of true positives divided by the number true positives plus false positives.
  • Recall is the number of true positives divided by the number of false negatives plus true positives.

  • The F-1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

docs.title: High Availability and Clustering
docs.text: Philter scales horizontally as a pool of stateless API nodes behind a load balancer, all sharing one cache and one database. High availability is a matter of topology and configuration, not special clustering code: you run more than one Philter instance, point them at a shared Valkey/Redis cache and the same MongoDB, and put a load balancer in front.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  clients["Your applications"]
  lb["Load balancer<br/>liveness: GET /api/health"]
  subgraph api["Stateless Philter API nodes (scale horizontally)"]
    p1["Philter node 1"]
    p2["Philter node 2"]
    p3["Philter node N"]
  end
  cache["Valkey / Redis<br/>shared cache: contexts, API keys"]
  db[("MongoDB<br/>system of record")]

  clients --> lb
  lb --> p1
  lb --> p2
  lb --> p3
  p1 --> cache
  p2 --> cache
  p3 --> cache
  p1 --> db
  p2 --> db
  p3 --> db

A load balancer distributes API requests across two or more identical, stateless Philter nodes. Every node reads and writes the same shared Valkey/Redis cache and the same MongoDB, so API requests can be served by any node. Consistent context replacements depend on retained MongoDB mappings and cache invalidation, as described below. Philter has no built-in UI, so there is no session-based component to pin to one node.

High availability needs MongoDB storage: set STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb on every node. SQLite storage, the default, keeps everything in one file used by one Philter instance, and refuses a second instance on the same file. A deployment that started on SQLite moves its data to MongoDB with the migrate-storage command before adding nodes; see Moving from SQLite to MongoDB.

docs.title: What is stateless and what is shared
docs.text:
• Philter API nodes are stateless. Each API request (/api/**) is authenticated from its own API key and depends on no server-side session, so any node can serve any request. Add or remove nodes freely.
  • MongoDB is the system of record. Policies, API keys, contexts and their token-to-replacement mappings, ledgers, and more live in MongoDB. Philter does not start without it.
  • Valkey/Redis is the shared cache. Context replacements and the API-key cache are shared through Valkey/Redis so they stay consistent across the fleet.

docs.title: Required configuration
docs.text:
Every node must share the same backing services:

  • Trusted proxies. List the load balancer's addresses in TRUSTED_PROXIES on every node, so each request is recorded, and rate limited, as coming from its client rather than the load balancer. See API Access.
  • Same cache. Set CACHE_HOSTNAME (and CACHE_PORT, CACHE_PASSWORD, CACHE_SSL as needed) identically on every node so they share one Valkey/Redis. With more than one node this is required: running several nodes without a shared cache is not a supported deployment. Without it, each node keeps its own in-process cache, invalidations do not reach the other nodes, and a revoked API key stays usable on other nodes until their cached copy expires. MongoDB still coordinates creation of new token mappings. The full configuration table is in Caching.
  • Same database. Set STORAGE_TYPE=mongodb and point every node at the same MongoDB. See Database.
  • Same encryption key. Set the same PHILTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY on every node. It is required to decrypt shared records, derive consistent keyed token hashes, and read what other nodes stored in the shared cache. Preserve it across restarts; see Encryption.
  • Same queue limits. Use identical async admission limits on every node.
  • Same policies. Because policies live in MongoDB, every node sees the same policies automatically once they share the database.

docs.title: Load balancing
docs.text:
Put any HTTP load balancer in front of the API nodes. Requests are stateless, so no sticky sessions are needed. Configure the load balancer health check against Philter's health endpoint:

GET /api/health

The health endpoint is a liveness check: it returns 200 with "status": "UP" when its handler can respond. It does not probe MongoDB, the cache, or worker progress. Remove unresponsive nodes from routing, but also monitor dependency availability, queue age, and processing failures before deciding a node can accept useful work. Philter does not expose a dedicated dependency-readiness endpoint through /api/health.

The Docker image serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate by default, which a load balancer will not trust. Hold the real certificate at the load balancer and set SSL_ENABLED=false on every node so they serve plain HTTP behind it, over a private network. See TLS.

docs.title: Horizontal scaling
docs.text:
• Add a node. Deploy another identical Philter instance with the same CACHE_HOSTNAME, database, and configuration, and register it with the load balancer. No data migration or rebalancing is needed, because the node holds no durable state of its own.
  • Remove a node. Drain it at the load balancer and stop it. Account for in-flight requests and background jobs before stopping it; see the ambiguous-outcome guidance below.
  • Sizing. Redaction throughput is CPU-bound, especially when policies use the name-detection (NER) filters. Size each node for your per-node request rate and scale the node count for total throughput; see System Requirements. Size the shared cache and database for the aggregate load of the whole fleet rather than per node.
  • Model serving. When policies use NER filters served by PhEye, PhEye is a separate scaling axis: Philter calls it for those filters, so scale PhEye alongside Philter for name-heavy workloads.

docs.title: Node failover
docs.text:
Shared state allows surviving nodes to continue processing, subject to dependency availability and recovery:

  • The load balancer stops routing to a node once its /api/health health check fails, and sends new requests to the remaining healthy nodes.
  • A lost connection leaves the outcome of an in-flight request uncertain. An async job may have been stored even if its acceptance response was lost; replaying the request can create another job. Philter has no general request idempotency key. If you received a document ID, check its status through the Documents API before resubmitting.
  • For context-scoped replacement, MongoDB atomically establishes mappings and supplies them on cache misses. Surviving nodes reuse retained mappings when keys, configuration, and invalidation are consistent. Eviction at MAX_CONTEXT_SIZE, explicit deletion or overwrite, and stale per-node caches can change that behavior; see Referential Integrity.
  • For explicit quota or contention rejections (429/503), honor Retry-After: 5 and use backoff. Persistent 503 may indicate an uncertain admission whose guard requires operator recovery. Follow the admission recovery procedure; do not clear the guard while any writer or database operation can still complete.

Make the shared services highly available too. Philter's own availability depends on the cache and database it shares, so run Valkey/Redis and MongoDB in their own highly-available configurations (for example, a replica set for MongoDB and a replicated or clustered Valkey deployment). A single-node cache or database is the real single point of failure in an otherwise horizontally-scaled Philter deployment.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Caching: the shared cache backend and its configuration.
  • Database: what Philter persists in MongoDB.
  • Referential Integrity: how consistent replacements work.
  • System Requirements: per-node sizing.

docs.title: Mistakes: Understanding Redaction Accuracy and Limitations
docs.text:
The information on this page is very important. If you have questions or would like clarification on anything discussed here, please contact us and we will be glad to assist.

Redaction is a critical process for protecting sensitive information, but it is important to understand that it is not an exact science. While Philter makes use of sophisticated technologies to identify and mask sensitive data, the process is inherently probabilistic and can occasionally result in mistakes.

docs.title: Redaction is Not a Scientific Process
docs.text:
Automated redaction involves the interpretation of human language, which is complex, nuanced, and often ambiguous. Because language does not follow a rigid set of mathematical rules, identifying sensitive information (like, but not limited to, names, addresses, or ages) requires balancing different methods of detection.

In document redaction, there are two primary types of errors:
